title: Truth-tellers, liars and contradiction
transcript: In a truth-teller puzzle, a person's type agrees with the truth of their statement. A truth-teller's statement is true, and a liar's statement is false. Turn each sentence into a short condition. Then combine the conditions before assigning everyone's type.

AMC logic practice can ask who made a correct statement or which claims can all hold at once. Keep a small table of cases. A Rossmoyne style argument may need to rule out every alternative. Use a contradiction if some proposed assignment cannot fit its own statements.
Everyone in a puzzle is either always truthful or always lies. Noor says: I am a liar. Can Noor say that consistently? Check what would happen under each of the two possible types.
If Noor is truthful, the claim of being a liar is false. That type cannot make the statement. If Noor is a liar, the claim is true. That also contradicts the type. Neither case works.
Two people are each truthful or a liar. Oli says that both of them are liars. Work out the types of both people. The second person makes no statement. Can the first claim its own type consistently?

If Oli were truthful, both would be liars by the statement. That contradicts the idea that Oli is truthful. The claim must be false. Since Oli really is a liar, the other person has to be truthful to make the pair different.
Noor says Oli is a liar. Oli says Pia is truthful. Pia says Raj is truthful. Raj says that Noor and Pia are different types. Everyone is either always truthful or always lies. Who is truthful?

A claim that someone is truthful makes the two types match. A claim that they lie makes the types opposite. Follow the first two links from Noor to Pia. Those two links make Noor and Pia opposite types. This determines the final statement without guessing any individual type. The statement by Raj is true. So Raj is truthful.

Now use the statement about Raj to identify Pia, which is truthful. Then Oli is truthful and Noor is a liar. Check each sentence with that assignment. The last statement fixed one type, and each link then forced the next, proving there is only one assignment.

A liar's entire stated sentence must be false. When the sentence says both people lie, one truthful person is enough to make it false. Checking one person's statement is a start. All statements must agree with the proposed types at the same time.

Mark each statement as a condition. Decide whether it gives same types, opposite types, or another relationship. Look for a type forced by several conditions. Then check the remaining assignments against all the statements.
